claim: Puromycin is a tyrosyl-tRNA mimic that blocks translation by labeling and releasing elongating polypeptide chains from translating ribosomes.
source: Puromycin is a tyrosyl-tRNA mimic that blocks translation by labeling and releasing elongating polypeptide chains from translating ribosomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about puromycin's mechanism of action.

claim: Puromycin has been used in molecular biology research for decades as a translation inhibitor.
source: Puromycin has been used in molecular biology research for decades as a translation inhibitor.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the use of puromycin in research.

claim: The development of puromycin antibodies and derivatized puromycin analogs has enabled the quantification of active translation in bulk and single-cell assays.
source: The development of puromycin antibodies and derivatized puromycin analogs has enabled the quantification of active translation in bulk and single-cell assays.
evidence: This statement describes the development and application of puromycin-based tools.

claim: In vivo puromycylation assays have become popular tools for localizing translating ribosomes in cells.
source: More recently, in vivo puromycylation assays have become popular tools for localizing translating ribosomes in cells.
evidence: This describes the current use of puromycylation assays in the field.

claim: Puromycylation assays often use elongation inhibitors to purportedly inhibit the release of puromycin-labeled nascent peptides from ribosomes.
source: These assays often use elongation inhibitors to purportedly inhibit the release of puromycin-labeled nascent peptides from ribosomes.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in puromycylation assays as reported in the literature.

claim: Even in the presence of elongation inhibitors, puromycylated peptides are released and diffuse away from ribosomes.
source: Using in vitro and in vivo experiments in various eukaryotic systems, we demonstrate that, even in the presence of elongation inhibitors, puromycylated peptides are released and diffuse away from ribosomes.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Puromycylation assays reveal subcellular sites, such as nuclei, where puromycylated peptides accumulate post-release.
source: Puromycylation assays reveal subcellular sites, such as nuclei, where puromycylated peptides accumulate post-release and which do not necessarily coincide with sites of active translation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental observations.

claim: Sites where puromycylated peptides accumulate do not necessarily coincide with sites of active translation.
source: Puromycylation assays reveal subcellular sites, such as nuclei, where puromycylated peptides accumulate post-release and which do not necessarily coincide with sites of active translation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in the study.

claim: Puromycin is a potent translational inhibitor that binds to ribosomes from all domains of life.
source: Puromycin is a potent translational inhibitor that binds to ribosomes from all domains of life and has been used as a chemical probe and selectable marker for decades (Aviner, 2020; Yarmolinsky and Haba, 1959).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Puromycin is itself a substrate of the ribosomal peptidyl-transferase reaction.
source: Puromycin is unique among translational inhibitors in that it is itself a substrate of the ribosomal peptidyl-transferase reaction (Nathans, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nathans, 1964.

claim: Puromycin mimics the 3′ adenosine of a tRNA charged with a modified tyrosine, which binds in the ribosomal acceptor site.
source: Puromycin mimics the 3′ adenosine of a tRNA charged with a modified tyrosine, which binds in the ribosomal acceptor site (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A showing the structural comparison.

claim: The ribosome transfers the nascent peptide chain on the P-site tRNA to puromycin, leading to spontaneous dissociation of the nascent peptide from the ribosome.
source: The ribosome transfers the nascent peptide chain on the P-site tRNA to puromycin, leading to spontaneous dissociation of the nascent peptide from the ribosome (Figure 1B; Nathans, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1B and a citation to Nathans, 1964.

claim: The development of anti-puromycin antibodies and derivatized analogs of puromycin has led to the commonplace use of puromycin as a metabolic probe to measure the extent of active translation.
source: The development of anti-puromycin antibodies and of derivatized analogs of puromycin (Fujiwara et al., 1982; Liu et al., 2012) has led to the commonplace use of puromycin as a metabolic probe to measure the extent of active translation, replacing radioactive tracers such as S35 methionine.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 1982 and Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Puromycin-based probes can be used to quantify the amount of active translation from cells in a culture dish, tissue or organism.
source: These probes can be used to quantify the amount of active translation from cells in a culture dish, tissue or organism (Schmidt et al., 2009; Chao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2009 and Chao et al., 2012.

claim: The ribopuromycylation method (RPM) claims to detect the subcellular localization of actively translating ribosomes using a puromycin-specific antibody.
source: Subsequent development of the ribopuromycylation method (RPM) (David et al., 2012; Bastide et al., 2018) pushed the technique a step further, claiming to detect the subcellular localization of actively translating ribosomes using a puromycin-specific antibody.
evidence: This describes claims made in previous publications, supported by citations.

claim: Authors of initial RPM publications argued that translation elongation inhibitors cycloheximide or emetine prevent dissociation of the puromycylated peptides from the ribosome.
source: In these initial publications, the authors argued that the translation elongation inhibitors cycloheximide or emetine prevent dissociation of the puromycylated peptides from the ribosome.
evidence: This describes claims made in previous publications.

claim: Cycloheximide and emetine bind in the E-site of the ribosome far from the peptidyl-transferase center.
source: Cycloheximide and emetine, however, bind in the E-site of the ribosome (Figure 1C) far from the peptidyl-transferase center (Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1C and citations to Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2014 and Wong et al., 2014.

claim: Cycloheximide and emetine prevent puromycin-induced splitting of ribosomes into individual subunits, but do not prevent the release of the majority of puromycylated peptides.
source: Previous work (Grollman, 1968; Colombo et al., 1965) established that these inhibitors prevent puromycin-induced splitting of ribosomes into individual subunits, but do not prevent the release of the majority of puromycylated peptides.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grollman, 1968 and Colombo et al., 1965.

claim: Cycloheximide and emetine are sometimes omitted from in vivo puromycylation assays based on the claim that short labeling times capture peptides near their original site of translation before significant diffusion has taken place.
source: Cycloheximide and emetine, in fact, are sometimes omitted from in vivo puromycylation assays based on the claim that short (approximately 5 min) labeling times capture peptides near their original site of translation before significant diffusion has taken place (tom Dieck et al., 2015; Biever et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2018; Glock et al., 2020; Holt et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes practices in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Puromycin-based imaging methods have been widely adopted, particularly in neurobiology, where translation in neuronal processes is crucial to neuronal function.
source: Puromycin-based imaging methods have been widely adopted, particularly in neurobiology, where translation in neuronal processes, far from the cell body, is crucial to neuronal function (tom Dieck et al., 2015; Biever et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2018; Glock et al., 2020; Holt et al., 2019; V'kovski et al., 2019; Langille et al., 2019; Gonatopoulos-Pournatzis et al., 2020; Graber et al., 2013; Graber et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the adoption of the method in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some studies have combined puromycin treatment with proximity-dependent ligation (PLA) to monitor the location of translation of a specific protein.
source: Some studies have combined puromycin treatment with proximity-dependent ligation (PLA) to monitor the location of translation of a specific protein (tom Dieck et al., 2015), but this method again does not address diffusion of puromycylated peptides post-release from the ribosome.
evidence: This describes a method used in previous studies, supported by a citation.

claim: Puromycin-based methods, as currently implemented, do not accurately localize translation at the subcellular level.
source: In the present work, we establish that puromycin-based methods, as currently implemented, do not accurately localize translation at the subcellular level.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Puromycin nearly instantaneously releases nascent proteins from the ribosome in rabbit reticulocyte lysate system.
source: We used a rabbit reticulocyte lysate system to show that puromycin nearly instantaneously releases nascent proteins from the ribosome, and that this release reaction is completely unaffected by emetine.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experiments.

claim: The release reaction of nascent proteins by puromycin is completely unaffected by emetine in rabbit reticulocyte lysate.
source: We used a rabbit reticulocyte lysate system to show that puromycin nearly instantaneously releases nascent proteins from the ribosome, and that this release reaction is completely unaffected by emetine.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experiments.

claim: Brief treatment with puromycin nearly completely dissociated nascent peptides from their mRNAs in cells, independent of the presence of emetine.
source: To validate this finding in cells, we visualized sites of active translation using fixed cell single-molecule imaging with the SunTag reporter system. Brief treatment with puromycin nearly completely dissociated nascent peptides from their mRNAs, again, independent of the presence of emetine.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's cellular experiments using the SunTag system.

claim: Released peptides could diffuse to nearly any point within even large mammalian cells within seconds or minutes according to simple diffusion calculations.
source: Simple diffusion calculations predict that the released peptides could diffuse to nearly any point within even large mammalian cells within seconds or minutes.
evidence: This is based on diffusion calculations presented in the study.

claim: Puromycylation methods described in the literature do not establish subcellular localization of translation.
source: Thus, puromycylation methods described in the literature do not establish subcellular localization of translation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) is a click-reactive cell permeable puromycin analog that is commonly used to localize sites of translation.
source: O-propargyl-puromycin (OPP) is a click-reactive cell permeable puromycin analog that is commonly used to localize sites of translation (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes OPP and its use, supported by a citation.

claim: When incubated with live cells or tissues, OPP reacts with translating ribosomes and becomes covalently attached to elongating peptides.
source: When incubated with live cells or tissues, OPP reacts with translating ribosomes and becomes covalently attached to elongating peptides.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of OPP labeling.

claim: OPP signal was most intense in nuclei, specifically in the chromatin-free center where nucleoli reside, in live C. elegans gonads.
source: Using this method to label translation in live C. elegans gonads, we observed bright labeling of live germlines upon a 5 min incubation with OPP. The OPP signal was most intense in nuclei, specifically in the chromatin-free center where nucleoli reside.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's experiments with C. elegans.

claim: A lower OPP signal was observed in the cytoplasm of C. elegans germlines, which contains the majority of (if not all) functional ribosomes.
source: A lower signal was also observed in the cytoplasm, which contains the majority of (if not all) functional ribosomes (Klinge and Woolford, 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, with a citation supporting the location of functional ribosomes.

claim: OPP labeling of nuclei was ablated by pre-treatment with anisomycin in C. elegans germlines.
source: OPP labeling of nuclei was ablated by pre-treatment with anisomycin, a competitive inhibitor of puromycin that stops elongation by binding to the peptidyl-transferase center (Grollman, 1967), thereby preventing puromycin from reacting with the nascent chain.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, with a citation supporting anisomycin's mechanism.

claim: OPP labeling was unaffected by pre-treatment with emetine in C. elegans germlines.
source: In contrast, OPP labeling was unaffected by pre-treatment with emetine (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Emetine-resistant puromycin labeling of nucleoli has been observed previously in tissue culture cells.
source: Emetine-resistant puromycin labeling of nucleoli has been observed previously in tissue culture cells (David et al., 2012) and may reflect trafficking or diffusion of puromycylated peptides into the nucleolus (Kubota et al., 1999; Schmidt et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Emetine-resistant puromycin labeling of nucleoli may reflect trafficking or diffusion of puromycylated peptides into the nucleolus.
source: Emetine-resistant puromycin labeling of nucleoli has been observed previously in tissue culture cells (David et al., 2012) and may reflect trafficking or diffusion of puromycylated peptides into the nucleolus (Kubota et al., 1999; Schmidt et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: OPP labels translational products but does not necessarily identify sites of active translation even in the presence of emetine.
source: We conclude that OPP labels translational products but does not necessarily identify sites of active translation even in the presence of emetine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the C. elegans experiments.

claim: Luciferase rapidly folds into an enzymatically active conformation only after release from the ribosome.
source: This method relies on the fact that luciferase rapidly folds into an enzymatically active conformation only after release from the ribosome (Kolb et al., 1994; Frydman et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolb et al., 1994 and Frydman et al., 1994.

claim: RRL programmed with truncated luciferase mRNA displays little luciferase activity compared to RRL translating full-length mRNA.
source: RRL programmed with the truncated mRNA (yellow trace) displays little luciferase activity compared to RRL translating full-length mRNA (purple trace).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's in vitro experiments, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of 91 μM puromycin causes a sharp increase in luminescence output from truncated luciferase mRNA, consistent with release of the stalled peptides.
source: Addition of 91 μM puromycin (the same concentration used by David et al., 2012) causes a sharp increase in luminescence output from the truncated mRNA, consistent with release of the stalled peptides.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experiments.

claim: The increase in luminescence observed upon puromycin addition was not inhibited by simultaneous addition of emetine in rabbit reticulocyte lysate.
source: Upon addition of puromycin to lysate programmed with truncated mRNA, we noticed the expected steep increase in luminescence (yellow trace) that was not inhibited by simultaneous addition of emetine (blue trace) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experiments, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Puromycin treatment caused a sharp increase in luminescence that was not affected by emetine pre-treatment but was inhibited by anisomycin pre-treatment in GDPNP-treated lysate.
source: Again, puromycin treatment (yellow trace) caused a sharp increase in luminescence that was not affected by emetine pre-treatment (blue trace) but was inhibited by anisomycin pre-treatment (green trace).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's in vitro experiments, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Pretreating translating ribosomes with emetine does not prevent the release of nascent peptides by puromycin in vitro.
source: Taken together, these results show that pretreating translating ribosomes with emetine does not prevent the release of nascent peptides by puromycin in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the in vitro experiments.

claim: The SunTag technique relies on a reporter mRNA encoding tandem repeats of the SunTag epitope near the 5′ end of the coding sequence.
source: This technique relies on a reporter mRNA encoding tandem repeats of the SunTag epitope near the 5′ end of the coding sequence (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes the SunTag method, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: When translated, each SunTag peptide is bound by a single chain variable fragment (scFV) of a GCN4 antibody fused to super folder GFP (scFV-sfGFP).
source: When translated, each SunTag peptide is bound by a single chain variable fragment (scFV) of a GCN4 antibody fused to super folder GFP (scFV-sfGFP).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the SunTag system.

claim: An auxin-inducible degron (AID) near the 3′ end of the coding sequence allows controlled degradation of the fully-synthesized SunTag array.
source: An auxin-inducible degron (AID) near the 3′ end of the coding sequence allows controlled degradation of the fully-synthesized SunTag array, reducing fluorescence background and enabling detection of single fully-synthesized polypeptides.
evidence: This describes a feature of the SunTag reporter system.

claim: In untreated cells, an average of 63% of single mRNAs per cell co-localize with bright SunTag signal.
source: In untreated cells, an average of 63% of single mRNAs (red foci) per cell co-localize with bright SunTag signal (green foci) (Figure 4B, top row and 4C); these co-localized spots reflect mRNAs bound by ribosomes synthesizing the SunTag reporter, while weaker isolated green spots reflect single fully synthesized SunTag polypeptides that have been released from the ribosome (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's cellular experiments, supported by Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Upon treatment with 91 μM puromycin for 5 min, an average of only 3% of mRNAs per cell colocalize with green signal.
source: Upon treatment with 91 μM puromycin for 5 min, an average of only 3% of mRNAs per cell colocalize with green signal, consistent with release of nascent chains upon puromycin treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's cellular experiments.

claim: Pre-treatment with 208 μM emetine for 15 min resulted in only 5% of mRNAs on average colocalizing with SunTag signal after puromycin treatment.
source: Remarkably, pre-treatment with 208 μM emetine for 15 min yielded similar results: only 5% of mRNAs on average colocalized with SunTag signal.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's cellular experiments.

claim: Pre-treatment for 5 min with elongation inhibitor anisomycin (37 μM) resulted in an average of 50% of mRNAs co-localized with green foci.
source: Importantly, pre-treatment for 5 min with elongation inhibitor anisomycin (37 μM), resulted in an average of 50% of mRNAs co-localized with green foci, as seen in untreated cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's cellular experiments.

claim: 5 min of puromycin treatment causes release of nascent polypeptides and diffusion away from ribosomes.
source: Together, these data indicate that 5 min of puromycin treatment causes release of nascent polypeptides and diffusion away from ribosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the SunTag experiments.

claim: Pre-treatment with emetine has no effect on puromycin-induced release of nascent polypeptides in cells.
source: Pre-treatment with emetine has no effect on puromycin-induced release.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the SunTag experiments.

claim: A protein is expected to diffuse ~100 µm in less than 1 min even in the most limiting case of one-dimensional diffusion.
source: However, even in the most limiting case of one-dimensional diffusion—approximating movement along a very narrow neural projection—a protein is expected to diffuse ~100 µm in less than 1 min.
evidence: This is based on diffusion calculations presented in the study, supported by Figure 5.

claim: The distance a protein can diffuse in minutes is large compared to the scale of relevant structures to which protein synthesis was localized in neurons (tens of microns).
source: This distance is large compared to both the scale of the relevant structures to which protein synthesis was localized in neurons (tens of microns) (tom Dieck et al., 2015; Biever et al., 2020), and to the diameter of HeLa cells (~20 microns) (Borle, 1969), in which the method was demonstrated (David et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diffusion calculations and comparison to cell dimensions, supported by citations.

claim: Limiting puromycin treatment time to a few minutes does not ensure that nascent proteins remain confined to the subcellular region in which they are synthesized.
source: Thus, limiting puromycin treatment time to a few minutes does not ensure that nascent proteins remain confined to the subcellular region in which they are synthesized.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diffusion calculations.

claim: The puromycin method for visualizing localized translation does not faithfully detect nascent polypeptides at the site of their synthesis.
source: In this work, we have demonstrated that the puromycin method for visualizing localized translation does not faithfully detect nascent polypeptides at the site of their synthesis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental findings.

claim: Puromycylated polypeptides are released from the ribosome and can diffuse far away from the site of synthesis, even following short treatment times.
source: Puromycylated polypeptides are released from the ribosome and can diffuse far away from the site of synthesis, even following short treatment times.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's experiments and diffusion calculations.

claim: Treatment with emetine does not prevent release of puromycylated peptides from the ribosome.
source: Additionally, treatment with emetine does not prevent release of puromycylated peptides from the ribosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's experiments.

claim: Neither emetine nor cycloheximide ultimately prevent release of puromycylated peptides according to previous polysome gradient analysis and real-time SunTag imaging.
source: This is in agreement with previous polysome gradient analysis (Colombo et al., 1965; Grollman, 1968) and real-time SunTag imaging (Wang et al., 2016) that has shown that neither emetine nor cycloheximide ultimately prevent release of these peptides.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The specific subcellular localizations detected by puromycylation methods are in many cases the end result of trafficking or diffusion of partially-synthesized puromycylated proteins.
source: It is therefore likely that the specific subcellular localizations detected by this method are in many cases the end result of trafficking or diffusion of partially-synthesized puromycylated proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: The bright nucleolar labeling detected in David et al., 2012 likely does not reflect nucleolar translation, but the trafficking of puromycylated N-terminal fragments of highly abundant ribosomal proteins to the nucleolus.
source: For example, the bright nucleolar labeling detected in David et al., 2012 likely does not reflect nucleolar translation, but the trafficking of puromycylated N-terminal fragments of highly abundant ribosomal proteins (which have N-terminal nucleolar localization signals) to the nucleolus (Kubota et al., 1999; Schmidt et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an interpretation of previous findings based on the current study's results, supported by citations.

claim: Conclusions reached using the puromycylation method should be treated cautiously, even in neurons.
source: Thus, conclusions reached using this method should be treated cautiously, even in neurons, where cellular projections protrude relatively far from the cell body.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Other reporter-based methods that rely on rapid, single turnover chemistry, such as the 'flash' activity of some luciferases, may allow for more accurate localization of the sites of protein synthesis.
source: We note that other reporter-based methods that rely on rapid, single turnover chemistry, such as the 'flash' activity of some luciferases, may allow for more accurate localization of the sites of protein synthesis (Na et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a suggestion for alternative methods, supported by a citation.

claim: Derivatizing puromycin with a chemical moiety large enough to obstruct its passage through the ribosome exit tunnel would immobilize reacted nascent chains on the ribosome.
source: Additionally, in principle, derivatizing puromycin with a chemical moiety large enough to obstruct its passage through the ribosome exit tunnel would immobilize reacted nascent chains on the ribosome.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal for improving the method.

claim: The viability of immobilizing nascent chains on the ribosome is demonstrated by the RiboLace method, which uses a puromycin-biotin conjugate bound to magnetic beads to capture translating ribosomes from cellular lysates.
source: The viability of this concept is demonstrated by the RiboLace method (Clamer et al., 2018), which uses a puromycin-biotin conjugate bound to magnetic beads to capture translating ribosomes from cellular lysates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clamer et al., 2018.

claim: RiboLace beads are not cell permeable and are unsuitable for in vivo imaging.
source: Of course, these beads are not cell permeable and are unsuitable for in vivo imaging.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the RiboLace method.

claim: Anisomycin is a competitive inhibitor of puromycin that stops elongation by binding to the peptidyl-transferase center.
source: OPP labeling of nuclei was ablated by pre-treatment with anisomycin, a competitive inhibitor of puromycin that stops elongation by binding to the peptidyl-transferase center (Grollman, 1967), thereby preventing puromycin from reacting with the nascent chain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grollman, 1967.

claim: The cytoplasm contains the majority of (if not all) functional ribosomes.
source: A lower signal was also observed in the cytoplasm, which contains the majority of (if not all) functional ribosomes (Klinge and Woolford, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Klinge and Woolford, 2019.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of GFP in the cytosol has been previously measured.
source: To determine how far a nascent protein might diffuse on these timescales (i.e. the spatial resolution of the method), we calculated the expected displacement as a function of time, based on the previously measured diffusion coefficient of GFP in the cytosol (Di Rienzo et al., 2014; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Di Rienzo et al., 2014.

claim: The diameter of HeLa cells is approximately 20 microns.
source: This distance is large compared to both the scale of the relevant structures to which protein synthesis was localized in neurons (tens of microns) (tom Dieck et al., 2015; Biever et al., 2020), and to the diameter of HeLa cells (~20 microns) (Borle, 1969), in which the method was demonstrated (David et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Borle, 1969.
